title: Infrastructure Engineering: GPU Fleet, Cloud Accounts, IaC Modules, CI/CD & Runbooks
author: Aisha Malik
content:
Overview
This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference infrastructure engineering guidance for GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines and build practices, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the canonical team wiki entry for cross-team engineers onboarding to infra and for oncall responders.

Scope and purpose
- Scope: global GPU fleet (hosted + dedicated), cloud account topology (AWS primary, GCP secondary), core Terraform modules, CI/CD build pipelines for runtime and infra modules, and runbooks for capacity incidents and rollouts.
- Purpose: reduce ambiguity in ownership, standardize IaC and CI/CD patterns, and provide concrete runbooks for common incidents (capacity pressure, network failures, Terraform drift, failed rollouts).

Ownership and contacts
- Infra Platform (primary): infra-platform@redwood.com, owner: Aisha Malik
- GPU Fleet SRE: Diego Ramirez
- Cloud Accounts & Networking: Priya Nair
- IaC Modules & CI/CD: Lena Novak
- Oncall escalation: see runbook section; paging via PagerDuty (infra-platform-oncall)

Key principles
- Single source of truth: Terraform modules in infra-repo are the canonical config for account networking and fleet provisioning.
- Small, composable modules: modules should do one thing (networking, compute, autoscaling, IAM), be well documented and versioned.
- Safe rollouts: changes to capacity or autoscaling must follow canary -> staged -> global with automated rollback.
- Observable and cost-aware: all services must emit cost tags and capacity metrics (GPU utilization, queue latency, token throughput).

GPU fleet and capacity planning
- KPIs and SLOs:
  - Node availability SLO: 99.95% per region (target), measured by healthy node count and ASG readiness.
  - Scheduling latency SLO: median pod startup < 300 ms for warm pools; cold-start median < 10 s.
  - Queue wait time SLO: 99th percentile request queue wait < 200 ms for dedicated customers.
- Capacity thresholds and actions:
  - Normal operating band: utilization 20-65% (sustained).
  - Warning band: 65-80% sustained for 30+ minutes -> trigger capacity add workflow and alert to capacity pager.
  - Critical band: >80% sustained for 15+ minutes -> immediate scale-up, enable burst capacity policy, and open incident.
- Capacity planning cadence:
  1) Weekly utilization review automated report (infra-metrics team).
  2) Monthly forecast: 90-day consumption curve, reserved capacity commitments, and cost modeling.
  3) QBR: present capacity headroom, forecast errors, and recommended purchases.
- Autoscaling & provisioning patterns:
  - Warm pool approach: maintain a pool of pre-warmed nodes to meet latency SLOs; warm pool target is derived from p99 throughput and cold-start cost.
  - Burst capacity policy: short-lived spot/ephemeral instances for traffic spikes; fallback to on-demand when spot unavailable.
  - Pod scheduling: prefer GPU-affinity nodes by model family label to maximize packing.

Sample capacity decision matrix (table)
| Condition | Metric | Action | Owner | Runbook ID |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Forecasted 30-day increase > 20% | Forecast delta (%) | Start procurement cycle for reserved capacity, schedule capacity ramp | Capacity PM | RB-001 |
| Sustained utilization 65-80% for 30m | GPU util (avg) | Increase warm pool by 10%, notify SRE | GPU Fleet SRE | RB-002 |
| >80% sustained 15m | GPU util (avg) | Immediate scale, enable burst, open incident | Oncall | RB-002 |

Cloud accounts and networking
- Account topology (high level):
  - Organization root -> Security account -> Shared services account -> Prod, Staging, Dev accounts per region
  - Dedicated customer VPCs are provisioned in customer-specific accounts when required by contract.
- VPC and peering standards:
  - Use private subnets for compute and NAT for outbound egress.
  - Transit gateway for region-to-region connectivity; avoid point-to-point peering at scale.
  - VPC CIDR allocations: standard 10.0.x.0/22 per account to reduce overlap.
- Firewall and security group baseline (table):
| Component | Allowed inbound | Allowed outbound | Notes |
| Runtime GPU nodes | 22 (bastion only), 5000-6000 (internal cluster ports) | 0.0/0 via NAT for egress only | Use ephemeral node security group, no public IPs for prod nodes |
| Control plane services | 443 from redwood subnets, 5432 from monitoring subnets | 443 to external endpoints as needed | Restrict by account role and KMS access |
- Network observability and tagging:
  - All resources must include tags: team, service, cost_center, env, owner.
  - VPC flow logs enabled to central logging account with 30-day default retention.

Terraform / IaC modules and patterns
- Module registry and repo layout:
  - Repo: infra-modules (mono-repo). Primary modules: vpc, subnet, transit-gateway, gpu-cluster, autoscaling, iam-roles, kms-keys.
  - Module versioning: semantic versions, changelog in module subdir, CI enforces module compatibility tests.
- Required module metadata (per module):
  - name, purpose, inputs list, outputs list, owner, supported providers, minimum tested version.
- Example module table:
| Module | Purpose | Owner | Stable version | CI job |
| vpc | Standardized VPC and subnets | Priya Nair | v1.8.0 | test-vpc-module |
| gpu-cluster | Provision GPU autoscaling groups, warm pools | Diego Ramirez | v2.4.1 | test-gpu-cluster |
| iam-roles | Centralized IAM roles and policies | Lena Novak | v1.2.3 | test-iam |
- IaC best practices:
  1) Keep state isolated per account using remote state (S3 + DynamoDB locking).
  2) Prefer data-driven modules with clear inputs and sensible defaults.
  3) Enforce pre-merge plan checks and differential approval for production changes.
  4) Run terraform fmt and tflint in CI; require 2 approvers for prod changes.

CI/CD and build practices
- Pipeline types:
  - Infra pipelines: validate plan -> policy checks (OPA), integration tests in sandbox -> apply with gate and manual approval for prod accounts.
  - Runtime service pipelines: build -> unit tests -> image build and scan -> gate to staging smoke tests -> canary rollout to prod clusters.
- Example infra pipeline steps (Terraform module change):
  1) PR opened -> CI runs terraform fmt, tflint, unit tests.
  2) CI runs terraform plan in a sandbox AWS account (ephemeral workspace).
  3) Automated policy checks (OPA, cost guardrails).
  4) Merge to main triggers integration tests.
  5) Apply to dev account automatically.
  6) For prod changes: create change request (CR) and require 2 approvers and scheduled maintenance window.
- Runtime pipeline example (service):
  - Build image with image tag = commit SHA; push to ECR; run image-scan; deploy to staging via ArgoCD; smoke tests; promote by tag to canary; monitor metrics for 30 minutes; if stable, promote to 50% and then 100%.
- CI artifacts and security:
  - All artifacts must be signed; container images scanned for critical vulnerabilities and blocked if threshold exceeded.
  - CI secrets are stored in Vault with least privilege.

Runbooks and incident procedures
- Runbook IDs: RB-001 capacity forecast, RB-002 immediate capacity incident, RB-003 node networking failure, RB-004 terraform drift detected
- Common incident runbook (RB-002 Immediate capacity incident):
  1) Alert fires on PagerDuty: infra-platform-oncall.
  2) Acknowledge and set incident channel (Slack #inc-infra-capacity).
  3) Run quick checks: current GPU utilization, node health, queue depth, recent autoscaler actions. Command examples:
     - kubectl get nodes -l gpu=true -o wide
     - promql: max_over_time(avg_over_time(gpu_utilization[5m])[15m:5m])
     - aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --region us-west-2 --query 'AutoScalingGroups[*].{Name:AutoScalingGroupName,Desired:DesiredCapacity,Instances:Instances}'
  4) If utilization > 80% and autoscaler unable to add capacity: enable burst policy (infractl capacity enable-burst --pool gpu-warm --region us-west-2) and notify capacity PM.
  5) If network errors present, follow RB-003.
  6) Post-incident: create incident review and update capacity forecast and runbook steps within 48 hours.

Terraform drift detection (RB-004):
- Daily drift job runs terraform plan against live state; if drift detected and not documented, open a ticket and create a notification to the owning team. Emergency remediation requires a change request and 2 approvers.

Oncall escalation and paging
- Primary pager: infra-platform-oncall (first responder 15 minutes).
- Escalation policy: 15m -> secondary -> 30m -> engineering lead -> 60m -> exec-level alert.
- Pager message template: include incident id, top 3 metrics (gpu util, queue length, pod restart rate), last deploy time, and active mitigations.

Change management and rollout guidance
- Canary procedure for infra changes touching capacity or autoscaling:
  1) Apply change to dev account.
  2) Apply to staging and run full load test (k6 / cluster-sim).
  3) Canary in prod: target 5% of traffic for 1 hour, monitor p50/p99 latency and error rate.
  4) If stable, increase to 25% for 2 hours, then full rollout.
  5) Automate rollback on metric regression with 5-minute stabilization window.

Known issues and mitigations
- GPU scheduling fragmentation: mitigate with node pooling by model family and binpacking labels.
- Spot capacity preemption: use mixed instances with on-demand fallback and warm pool redundancy.
- Terraform state contention: enforce per-account state isolation and DynamoDB locks; where contention recurs, investigate module granularity.

Appendices
- Useful commands:
  - infractl status --account prod-us-west-2 --resource-type gpu
  - infractl plan --module gpu-cluster --account staging
  - aws s3 cp s3://infra-state-prod/terraform.tfstate ./tfstate --profile infra-readonly
- Metrics to monitor (minimal list): gpu_utilization, pod_startup_latency_ms, queue_wait_ms_p99, node_boot_time_s, terraform_plan_fail_rate
- Related pages and runbooks: see related_pages metadata above.
